Heres how it works.  Simplified 

The total treasury marketable securities outstanding are owned by two players.  The Fed and the private sector.  Let's clown what's outstanding as 2's and 30's only. 

Total outstanding is 100 units of which 70 units is 2's and 30
Units is 30.  The Wam is (2*70+30*30)/100=10.4 years

Let's say the Fed owns 20% of the total. And is 50/50 that means they hold 16 years of WAM   

The other 80% has to be shorter WAM than 10.4. Turns out is (10.4*100-16*20)/80=9 years 

Ignoring the treasury for the moment.  In order for the Fed wam to go to 10.4 fron 16 they would need to sell 20% of their 30's and buy 20% more twos and they would have to have the private sector take those on such that the private sector WAM would rise.   That rise from 9 to 10.4 would force more risk on the private sector and tighten. 

However the Fed doesn't actually sell it lets its holdings mature and buys new 2's and 30's from the treasury and maintains its 16 WAM.  The treasury can maintain its 10.4 Wam by issuing 9 Wam to the private sector.  IF the Fed unilaterally stopped buying as much 30's such that their wam would fall toward 10.4 over time UNLESS the treasury increased what it sold to the private sector the impact of the Fed change would have no private sector impact and no tightening.  However the Fed's action would impact the total wam issued by treasury downward from 10.4 toward 9.  The treasury would have to decide if that's desirable or not.  If not they would increase private sector 30 year auctions and tighten.  The Fed can do whatever it wants but ONLY if the treasury adjusts to those changes and issues more 30'z to the private sector (so as to maintain their overall wam) will there be a tightening impact of the Fed shift 

The attached chart shows the actual wam of SOMA, private sector and overall which illustrates how the high wam of the soma portfolio suppresses yields by starving the private sector of duration

Just some TLDR notes on $AAOI earnings:

- Expects full qualification of 1.6T products by their hyperscaler customer within next couple of weeks 

(helpful revenue ramp #2, timelines)

-  Continues to believe that AOI will have the largest AI DC transceiver production capacity in the US
 
(reiterating ambitions during a time when their competitors might get banned)

- Expects facilities toward InP capacity to come online in early 2027 

(timeline FYI in terms of further ramp) 

- Total capacity is approaching 200,000/u per month, EOY 650,000/u per month of 800g/1.6t. EOY 2027, 930,000/u 

(this is the ramp i want to see)

- "increase our manufacturing capacity for our external light source or ELSFP. That's for co-packaged optics or CPO". we anticipate ramping production later this year and into 2027, ultimately culminating in about 400,000 pieces per month in 2028

(need some time to model this into revenue)

- "As we have mentioned before, we've been manufacturing lasers internally for many years. This has allowed us to avoid some of the shortages that  have affected others in the industry"

(vertical integration bull case during CW/EML laser shortages) 

- We believe that in the future, CPO will continue to drive increased demand for high-power lasers

(thesis validation on CPO sector)

- "to our long-term objective of returning non-GAAP gross margins to around 40%"

-  "We ended the second quarter with $508.8 million in total cash equivalents"

I need to double check if the ATM finished or not

- "our ability to deliver revenue in general, and specifically when it  comes to 800G products, is limited by our production capacity right now" "If we could produce more, we could ship more right now"

Demand > Supply validation. 

- "Most of the increased capacity will be in U.S. Even so, let me say that, like I keep emphasizing, that is not good enough for the customer demand. The customer demand is 20%-40% higher."

Unholy photonics demand validation across the whole sector, read through for $LITE, $SIVE / $JBL, and others is amazing. 

- "Not in the next two, three years, especially the demand is so big. Okay?  Even combined AI, $LITE, $COHR, $AVGO all together, it's still very tough to meet the customer demand in the next few years"

More optical sector demand validation. 

- CPO Timelines: "If you're talking about really high volume manufacturer [for CPO market], I would say more like the late Q3 next year" and "We have been working very close with at least five customer"

If you care about current earnings (which I'm not really looking at closely)

Revenue: $191M vs. $190m 
EPS: $.06 vs. $.02

TLDR: Extraordinary demand across the laser + optical sector read through. Kinda supporting Lumentum CEO statement that laser shortage is worse than memory shortages. 

2027 capacity ramp on track. To map inflection period with timelines, would be around early next year, as stated in their previous earnings call. 

AAOI has the customers now. Limitation is making enough lasers and transceivers.

TL;DR

- The bottleneck for AI is no longer money—it’s power. Capital is abundant, but electricity, transformers, GPUs, cooling, networking and data centres are the scarce resources limiting AI growth. 

- Energy and AI can both be broken into four layers: Make, Move, Store, Sell. This framework helps identify where value will accrue across the stack. 

- For electricity, these correspond to generating power, transmitting it, storing it (batteries/thermal storage), and selling it through utilities and power markets. 

- For AI, they correspond to creating models and chips, networking and interconnects, memory and context storage, and finally applications and APIs that sell intelligence. 

-We are at an inflection point because AI demand has exploded, energy technologies (especially solar and batteries) have become economically viable, governments now view AI and energy as strategic priorities, and a new generation of founders has emerged to build hard-tech companies. 

- The biggest long-term winners will be systems companies that vertically integrate hardware, software, energy and operations rather than pure software businesses. 

- Today’s infrastructure bottlenecks - GPUs, transformers, cooling, networking and power equipment - are tomorrow’s platforms. The biggest companies will emerge by solving these constraints, not simply exploiting them temporarily. 

- Compute factories (next-generation AI data centres) are becoming the “refineries” of the AI era, manufacturing intelligence by integrating power, cooling, networking, chips and software into one system. 

- AI is accelerating an enormous buildout across energy infrastructure, batteries, compute markets and frontier power technologies (SMRs, geothermal, fusion, etc.), compressing decades of learning into just a few years.

- The core investment thesis is simple: intelligence is humanity’s highest-return asset, so the biggest opportunities lie in companies that lower the cost of producing intelligence - or the energy required to create it.
